questions.q: Which of these is the best definition of master data, per this lesson?
options: The core business entities — customers, products, vendors, employees, locations — that multiple systems and processes share and reuse
Any data that is backed up to a secondary location
The raw log files generated by a web server
Data that has been deleted but not yet purged
questions.explain: Master data is defined by being the core, reusable entities an organization refers to repeatedly across many systems — not by backup status, log format, or deletion state.

questions.q: Which trait does this lesson NOT list as characteristic of master data?
options: It is reused across many systems and processes rather than generated once
It typically changes very slowly compared to transactional data
It is relatively low in volume but high in value
It grows by the second, the way a transaction log does
questions.explain: Fast, continuous growth is explicitly the trait of transactional data, used in the lesson as the contrast to master data's slow rate of change.

questions.q: In the 'Robert Chen / Bob Chen / R. Chen' example, what is the core problem being illustrated?
options: The company has three different real customers who happen to share a phone number
One real customer is represented inconsistently across three systems, and no single system has the full, current picture
The phone number field was deleted from the database
The billing system has no record of this customer at all
questions.explain: All three systems refer to the same real person, but each has a partial or outdated view — exactly the scattered-entity problem MDM exists to resolve.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when do master data problems typically become visible?
options: They are visible immediately and constantly in daily operations
Never — they have no real business impact
At a specific moment, such as a merger, an audit, or a campaign that contacts the same customer multiple times
Only when a system goes offline entirely
questions.explain: The lesson describes master data problems as invisible day-to-day but suddenly very visible at a triggering event like a merger or a duplicate-contact campaign.

questions.q: Per this lesson's course roadmap, what does Chapter 2 focus on?
options: Specific master data domains like customer and product
Matching and consolidation — finding and merging duplicate views of the same entity
Reference data governance
MDM tooling vendors
questions.explain: Chapter 1 covers foundational vocabulary; Chapter 2 is described as going deep on matching and consolidation, the mechanics of finding and merging duplicate records.
